messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mohammad is a 54-year-old Middle Eastern man who has been seeking help after enduring years of physical abuse by his romantic partner. A community organizer by profession, Mohammad’s life has been deeply affected by the traumatic events he experienced at home. The incident that set off this cycle occurred late one evening in their apartment. The darkness and spatial triggers associated with the location have since become potent reminders of the violence he endured. As the physical abuse intensified, Mohammad began to experience auditory triggers—specifically, sounds reminiscent of helicopters or aircraft. These sounds now instantly bring back vivid memories of the frightening event. Mohammad’s memory of the incident is fragmented; the events come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, making it difficult for him to process and understand what happened. When he has these memories, he sometimes hears things in his head that he heard during the traumatic event, which can be triggered without warning by something in his surroundings. This unrelenting memory pattern has led him to develop hypervigilance towards people, particularly those who might pose a danger to him. The fragmented nature of his memories exacerbates his feelings of betrayal and character blame. Mohammad is certain that the abuse was a result of his own flaws—that he somehow deserved it due to being the sort of person he is. This belief has also shattered his previous understanding of how the world works, leading to a deep sense of mistrust in others. These negative appraisals have become deeply ingrained and have led him to avoid the site of the event at all costs. The physical locations where the abuse took place trigger intense memories that are both painful and confusing. In response, he has started wearing concealing clothing to avoid drawing attention to himself and potentially triggering further incidents. Over time, these maladaptive strategies have reinforced his negative appraisals and triggers. Mohammad’s hypervigilance towards dangerous people has made him more prone to feeling betrayed by others, as he constantly anticipates another instance of violence. The avoidance behaviors and concealing clothing have also contributed to his sense of isolation and mistrust. In his role as a community organizer, the environment in which he interacts with various groups has become fraught with danger signals. He avoids certain areas where the spatial triggers are most potent and often wears baggy clothes when attending events or meetings. This hypervigilance has strained his relationships both at work and at home, leading to increased tension and a sense of alienation. What finally brought Mohammad to seek help was an incident at a community event that closely resembled one of the traumatic triggers—a helicopter flying overhead triggered a full memory recall, complete with auditory intrusions. This left him feeling overwhelmed and unable to function. He is most afraid of losing control in public spaces and having another episode where he relives the abuse. At the same time, he hopes for a way to regain his sense of safety and trust in others. The tightening cycle of triggers, memories, negative appraisals, and maladaptive strategies has left Mohammad feeling trapped. He seeks help to break free from this pattern and reclaim his life without the constant fear and betrayal that now color every aspect of it.
